title: Widows and orphans have a claim on the Lord’s storehouse
setting: On 30 April 1832, Joseph Smith sat in council with Church leaders in Independence, Missouri. Days earlier he had visited the Colesville Saints in Kaw Township, about twelve miles west. That settlement included widows such as Phebe Peck and Anna Rogers. The Joseph Smith Papers editors think contact with these families likely raised a question. Under consecration, what claim did a widow have on property her husband had given the Church?
summary: The revelation adds to the Church’s laws for women and children who have lost husbands or fathers. Wives have a claim on their husbands for support until the husbands die. Faithful widows keep fellowship in the Church; unfaithful ones lose it but may stay on their inheritances under the law of the land. Children have a claim on their parents until they come of age. After that, they have a claim on the Lord’s storehouse if their parents cannot give them inheritances. The storehouse is kept by consecrations, and it provides for widows, orphans, and the poor.

contextNote.title: A widow’s land under two sets of laws
contextNote.text: Consecration raised a hard case: what if a widow’s husband had deeded their land to the Church? Verse 2 makes her fellowship depend on her own faithfulness. Verse 3 adds that even without fellowship, she “may remain upon” her inheritance. The phrase “according to the laws of the land” ties Church practice to Missouri law. Verse 6 then names the storehouse as the support for widows and orphans. In this passage, an inheritance is a family’s land that Church discipline alone does not take away.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 81–83, “Much Is Given Much Is Required,” connects this section with caring for those in need. Who in verses 4–6 has a claim on the storehouse, and in what order?
reviewNote: Read all 6 verses. Heading gives Independence, 30 April 1832, in council. JSP historical introduction gives the Kaw Township visit (28–29 April), the widows Phebe Crosby Peck and Anna Slade Rogers, Missouri dower law, and January 1833 publication. The link between the visit and the question is the JSP editors’ inference (“likely”); the setting presents it as context, not proven cause. Kaw Township is not in the gazetteer and was not added. Fact-check 2026-10-12: no changes
